claim: Forebrain/SCN-specific Bmal1 knockout mice were generated by crossing floxed Bmal1 mice with Camk2a::iCreBAC mice.
source: To generate a forebrain-specific knockout of circadian rhythms, we crossed floxed Bmal1 (Bmal1fx/fx) mice (Johnson et al., 2014) to Camk2a::iCreBAC mice (CamiCre or Cre) (Casanova et al., 2001) and produced CamiCre+; Bmal1fx/fx (that we denote as 'Brain' Knockout, BKO, defined as a forebrain-specific knockout) as well as Bmal1fx/fx (Fx/Fx), CamiCre+ (Cre), and CamiCre+; Bmal1fx/+ (Het) control mice.
evidence: The text explicitly describes the genetic crossing strategy used to generate the experimental mice, citing the source of the parental lines.

claim: Camk2a::iCreBAC mice express Cre in a neuron-specific, forebrain-enriched pattern that is highly expressed in the SCN.
source: Camk2a::iCreBAC mice were used because their Cre expression is faithful to the endogenous Camk2a gene expression pattern: it is neuron-specific, forebrain-enriched (Casanova et al., 2001), and expressed highly in the SCN as observed in Cre-dependent fluorescence reporter mice, CamiCre+; tdTom+ (Figure 1A–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work and by fluorescence reporter data shown in Figure 1A-E.

claim: Cre expression in Camk2a::iCreBAC mice is postnatal and starts at P3.
source: The other advantage of this Cre driver is that its Cre expression is post-natal and starts at P3 (Casanova et al., 2001), thus reducing potential developmental effects.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to the original characterization of the Cre line.

claim: The SCN in the hypothalamus is the primary regulator of daily rhythms of behavior and physiology in mammals.
source: The suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) in the hypothalamus is the primary regulator of daily rhythms of behavior and physiology in mammals (Meijer and Rietveld, 1989; Ralph et al., 1990; Sujino et al., 2003; Welsh et al., 2010), yet the majority of tissues in the body possess autonomous cellular oscillators (Yamazaki et al., 2000; Abe et al., 2002; Nagoshi et al., 2004; Welsh et al., 2004; Yoo et al., 2004; Abraham et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research establishing the role of the SCN.

evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations describing the molecular mechanism of the circadian clock.
